title: Reentrancy — Vulnerable Pattern and Fix
Cross-Function Reentrancy
content: Cross-function reentrancy re-enters a DIFFERENT function of the same contract instead of the same one, so a naive per-function guard does not help. Example: function A transfers ETH out (external call), then sets a flag; function B checks the flag and returns early. An attacker re-enters B from A's external call before the flag is set, bypassing the check. Mitigations: one guard covering the whole contract (a single shared nonReentrant state), CEI in every function, and locks on shared state. Pattern class: Reentrancy. Severity: high.

title: Token Callback Reentrancy (ERC-777 / ERC-1155)
content: Standards that notify recipients via callbacks open a reentrancy vector: ERC-777 tokens call tokensReceived() on the recipient and ERC-1155 calls onERC1155Received(). If the receiving contract uses those callbacks to re-enter the sender's logic mid-transfer (before state settles), it can double-spend or drain. The Uniswap v1 ETH-to-token conversion and several 2021-2022 exploits used ERC-777 hooks this way (e.g. the 2021 CREAM/Impossible Finance incident used the ERC-777 callback). Defense: CEI ordering, reentrancy guards on every state-changing function, and avoiding untrusted hook recipients. Pattern class: Reentrancy. Severity: critical.

title: Integer Overflow / Underflow — Vulnerable Pattern
tx.origin Authorization Misuse — Vulnerable Pattern
Unchecked External Call Return Values — Vulnerable Pattern
delegatecall to Untrusted Callee — Vulnerable Pattern
content:
delegatecall executes the callee's code in the CALLER's storage context, so a delegatecall to an untrusted address lets that address rewrite any storage variable — owner, balances, anything. The 2016 Parity wallet multi-sig hack destroyed ~$150M of ETH through an unprotected delegatecall. Vulnerable pattern:
```solidity
function execute(address target, bytes calldata data) external {
    target.delegatecall(data); // runs in THIS contract's storage
}
```
Guard the target address, keep proxy storage collision-free, and never let users supply arbitrary delegatecall targets. Pattern class: Business-Logic / Access-Control. Severity: critical.

title: Missing Access Control on Privileged Functions
content:
Access-control failures rank first in OWASP's smart-contract top 10: mint/fee/pause/upgrade functions left callable by anyone because the owner modifier is missing:
```solidity
function mint(address to, uint256 amount) external { // no onlyOwner
    _mint(to, amount); // anyone can mint unlimited supply
}
```
In 2024-2025 incident data, access-control flaws caused the largest dollar losses of any class. Every state-changing admin function needs an explicit role check and a test that unprivileged callers revert. Pattern class: Access-Control. Severity: critical.

title: Proxy Upgrade Storage Collision
content: Upgradeable contracts store implementation logic behind a proxy, but if a new implementation declares a variable occupying a slot already used by the proxy or an earlier implementation, values silently corrupt — balances, owners, and settings read garbage. Vulnerable pattern: adding a new state variable at the start of an inherited layout or reusing an EIP-1967 admin slot. Mitigations: structured proxy patterns (transparent/UUPS), storage-layout diff checks in CI, and timelocked upgrades. Pattern class: Storage-Collision. Severity: high.

title: Forced ETH and Selfdestruct Balance Surprises
content: Any contract that assumes its ETH balance can only change via its own payable functions is wrong: an attacker can force-send ETH via selfdestruct(addr) (pre-2022) or by pre-funding a CREATE2 address. This breaks invariant-based logic (e.g. share pricing that divides by balance), lets attacker manipulate accounting that reads address(this).balance, and can brick withdrawal loops. Auditors check that balance-based math accounts for forced ETH. Pattern class: Business-Logic. Severity: medium.

title: Denial of Service in Smart Contracts
content: Smart-contract DoS blocks protocol function: unbounded loops hitting the block gas limit, a single external call that always fails (transfer to a contract that rejects ETH), front-runnable initialization, or data structures that grow until operations exceed gas. For tokens, a blacklist that bricks a required function or fee-on-transfer breaking pool accounting are DoS variants. DoS often locks user funds indefinitely without an obvious 'hack'. Audit: every loop, every required external call, every initialization is a DoS candidate; prefer pull-based withdrawals. Pattern class: Business-Logic / Timing. Severity: high.

title: Vyper nonreentrant Compiler Bug (Curve 2023)
content: In July 2023, a Vyper compiler bug (versions 0.2.15-0.2.16) broke the @nonreentrant decorator: the reentrancy lock flag was not properly set, so guarded functions on affected contracts were re-entrant. This enabled the Curve pool exploits (alETH/ETH, pETH/ETH, msETH/ETH, CRV/ETH) that drained over $60M total, including read-only reentrancy variants in the aftermath. Lesson: guard implementations are only as good as the compiler; verify which compiler version + optimizer settings a contract used and whether that build had known bugs. Pattern class: Reentrancy / Supply-Chain. Severity: critical.

title: Flash-Loan Governance Attack (Beanstalk Pattern)
content: A flash-loan governance attack buys voting power for one block and passes a malicious proposal without owning a lasting stake. The canonical case is Beanstalk Farms (April 2022, ~$182M): the attacker flash-loaned Beans and ETH, used it to acquire governance voting weight (Stalk), passed a proposal that transferred protocol funds to themselves, then repaid the flash loan in the same transaction. Defense: time-locked proposals, quorum requirements that cannot be met by a single flash-loan-sized stake, vote-weight vesting, and emergency pause mechanisms. Pattern class: Flash-Loan + Access-Control. Severity: critical.

title: Just-in-Time (JIT) Liquidity MEV on Uniswap v3
content: JIT liquidity is an MEV strategy on concentrated-liquidity AMMs: right before a large swap, a bot adds concentrated liquidity inside the swap's price range, capturing a large share of the swap fees, then removes the position immediately after. The victim's swap is sandwiched between the JIT position open and close, so the bot earns fees with near-zero inventory risk while the trader gets worse execution. Detection: examine positions opened and closed within the same block around large swaps. Mitigation for LPs is difficult; routers can batch or MEV-protect swaps. Pattern class: MEV. Severity: medium.

title: Time-Bandit Attacks (Reorg MEV)
content: A time-bandit attack is MEV via chain reorg: a powerful miner/validator sees a profitable transaction (e.g. a large liquidation or arbitrage) in the mempool, reorgs the chain to exclude it, and replays the opportunity for itself. Time-bandits threaten settlement finality and are a reason protocols use auction-style or commit-reveal settlement for high-value liquidations. They are rare but catastrophic; private order flow and PBS reduce the attack surface. Pattern class: MEV / Timing. Severity: high.

title: Curve / Stable-Swap Pool Gotchas
content: Curve-style stable-swap pools use a hybrid constant-sum/constant-product curve that keeps price flat near the peg, which is what makes them efficient for stablecoins — and a manipulation target. Because a small amount of one asset can move a large pool's balance, spot prices from Curve pools are manipulable with a flash loan (Harvest Finance 2020 and many oracle exploits used Curve pools). The 2023 Vyper bug also hit Curve pools specifically. When a protocol prices from a Curve pool, check for TWAP, deviation guards, and whether the referenced pool has deep liquidity on BOTH sides. Pattern class: Oracle-Manipulation. Severity: high.

title: Aave / Compound-Style Lending Gotchas (eMode, Isolation)
content: Lending protocols add risk-model parameters that change exploit surface: efficiency mode (eMode) allows higher LTV for correlated assets, isolation mode caps exposure of novel assets, and oracle-address configuration determines what price a position liquidates against. Correlated-asset eMode baskets are exposed when the correlation breaks (both assets drop together). Watch liquidation thresholds, collateral factors, and oracle sources per asset; a flash-loan oracle manipulation that moves one collateral asset's price can cascade liquidations. Pattern class: Oracle-Manipulation / Business-Logic. Severity: high.

title: Uniswap v2-Style AMM Gotchas
content: Uniswap v2-style pools (constant product x*y=k) have known gotchas: (1) sync()/reserves can be manipulated by direct token transfers that skip the swap path; (2) flash swaps let anyone borrow the whole pool for one block; (3) fee-on-transfer / rebase tokens break reserve accounting because the pool receives less than the swap math assumes; (4) spot price = ratio of reserves, trivially manipulable on thin pools. Integrations should use TWAP or external oracles and measure post-transfer balances. Pattern class: Oracle-Manipulation / Business-Logic. Severity: high.

title: Uniswap v3-Style Concentrated Liquidity Gotchas
content: Uniswap v3 concentrated liquidity changes the attack surface: (1) tick-level ranges concentrate liquidity, so TWAPs over short windows can be manipulated with small capital by moving price within an empty range; (2) a single large position exiting can shift price violently; (3) JIT liquidity (see k3-defi-jit-liquidity) taxes large swaps; (4) fee tiers change routing economics. Protocols that read v3 spot prices or short TWAPs from thin tick ranges are exploitable. Check the liquidity distribution across ticks, not just total TVL. Pattern class: Oracle-Manipulation / MEV. Severity: high.

title: Liquidation Racing and Keeper Risk
content: Liquidation is a race: the first liquidator to close an underwater position earns the bonus, so MEV bots bid to win it. This creates (1) unfairness for small liquidators, (2) cascades when many positions share one price feed, and (3) 'liquidation honeypots' where a manipulated oracle triggers a wave of forced sells. Protocols mitigate with partial liquidations, price-change bounds, and auction-style mechanisms; traders under-collateralized by volatile assets should expect to be liquidated at a loss. Pattern class: MEV / Timing. Severity: medium.

title: Solana Account Confusion and Missing Signer Checks
content: Solana programs take all state as explicit accounts, so security depends on validating them: an attacker can pass the wrong account (a fake mint, a fake token account) unless the program checks owner, key, and signer. Common bugs: missing is_signer on a privileged account, missing owner check on a mint/account, and PDA seeds not derived from the expected program. The 2021 Wormhole exploit and several Solana bridge/program incidents stemmed from insufficient account/signature validation. Audit pattern: every account in an instruction must be validated for key, owner, and signer. Pattern class: Access-Control. Severity: critical.

title: Solana CPI and Reentrancy Safety
content: Cross-program invocations (CPI) on Solana call another program; unlike EVM, the callee cannot call back into the caller's code mid-CPI in the same way, but reentrancy-style issues still exist via state changed between a CPI and a later check, and via programs that call themselves or invoke untrusted programs with mutable accounts. Best practice: validate all accounts before any CPI, mark seeds properly, close accounts carefully, and treat any CPI target as a potential attacker. Auditors also check for missing 'close account' rent-reclaim logic. Pattern class: Reentrancy / Business-Logic. Severity: high.

title: Solana DEX Gotchas (Jupiter, Raydium)
content: Solana DEX routing has distinct gotchas: (1) Jupiter-style aggregators route across pools, so the executed route defines the risk — a token can be 'listed' through one scam pool; (2) Raydium CLMM (concentrated) pools have tick-range exposure like Uniswap v3; (3) serum/order-book venues have different depth profiles than AMMs; (4) priority fees determine MEV ordering on Solana, and Jito bundles enable atomic MEV. When analyzing Solana tokens, verify the mint's extensions (Token-2022), the pool's actual reserves, and whether the 'price' comes from a real pool or a thin/one-sided market. Pattern class: Business-Logic / MEV. Severity: high.

title: L2 Bridge Withdrawal Delays and Sequencer Risk
content: Bridging to/from rollups involves delays and trust assumptions: optimistic rollups require a challenge window (days) for withdrawals, ZK rollups prove validity but still rely on the bridge contract, and the sequencer can reorder or censor transactions until forced-inclusion is used. MEV and arbitrage across the L1-L2 boundary must account for the withdrawal delay; 'fast bridges' that front liquidity absorb that risk and can become insolvent if the canonical bridge is slow. For token analysis, check which bridge a wrapped asset uses and its trust model. Pattern class: Bridge-Exploit / Timing. Severity: high.

title: Tax / Fee Mutability as a Rug Vector
content: A token that launches with low buy/sell taxes and lets the owner RAISE taxes later is a honeypot-in-waiting: after buyers commit, the owner sets sell tax to 90%+ or adds a blacklist, trapping holders. Check for setTax / updateFee / setBlacklist functions and who can call them; renounced ownership is only meaningful if the dangerous functions are actually locked. On-chain tells: an ownership transaction shortly after launch that changes transfer logic. Severity: critical.

title: Fake Audit and Fake Partnership Red Flags
content: Scam projects fabricate legitimacy: 'audited by X' when no audit exists (or the audited code is not the deployed bytecode), fake partnership logos, fake exchange listings, and fake team credentials. Verification: check the auditor's site/registry directly, compare the audited commit with the deployed bytecode, and confirm partnerships from the partner's own channels. A claimed audit from an unknown firm or a screenshot of an audit is a strong scam signal. Severity: high.

title: Renounced Ownership Through an Upgradeable Proxy
content: A token can appear safe — ownership renounced on the PROXY — while the IMPLEMENTATION retains a minter or admin, or the proxy admin still controls upgrades. The renouncement is cosmetic: the deployer upgrades the implementation to one that steals balances or blocks sells. Always check three layers: proxy admin, implementation owner, and any roles in the implementation itself. Upgradeable tokens without a timelock are rug-able regardless of the current code. Severity: critical.

title: Liquidity Bootstrapping and Presale Rug Patterns
content: Liquidity bootstrapping pools (LBPs) and presales are rug-friendly: a 'fair launch' can end with the deployer withdrawing the pool, or a presale contract can fail to ever list the token. Red flags: presale deposits to a plain EOA, no audited sale contract, 'refundable' presales with no refund mechanism in code, and LBP weight changes that let insiders buy cheap. Verify the sale contract's logic (who can withdraw, when listing happens) and the LP add after the sale. Severity: high.

title: Slippage Trap and Fake-Liquidity Tokens
content: Some scam tokens make buys look possible but execution is a trap: the pool is one-sided or microscopically thin, so a 'successful' buy fills at a tiny fraction or the quote never executes; or the contract inflates the displayed price while the real pool is empty. Check the pool's actual reserves on-chain and simulate the exact swap before buying. A token whose chart shows volume but whose pool has $100 of real liquidity is not tradeable — it is a trap. Severity: critical.

title: Solana Account Model for Analysis
content: Solana's account model differs from EVM: every asset (mint, token account, program, PDA) is a separate account owned by a program, and transactions list all accounts explicitly. For token analysis this means: check the mint authority (can it mint more?), the freeze authority, and Token-2022 extensions; check LP positions as NFT/positions with explicit ranges; and verify program ownership of accounts. Rent, priority fees, and Jito bundles shape transaction patterns. Solscan and similar explorers expose these fields. Severity: informational.

title: Token-2022 Extensions Risk Catalogue
content: Solana's Token-2022 standard adds extensions that change risk: transfer fees (token takes a cut of every transfer — can be set to trap sellers), transfer hooks (custom code on every transfer — can blacklist/block), confidential transfers, metadata, and permanent delegate. A 'normal-looking' Token-2022 mint can carry a transfer hook that reverts sells for most addresses — a programmable honeypot. Inspect the mint's extension list and the hook program before interacting. Severity: critical.

title: Verifying LP Locks and Lock Contracts
content: Locked liquidity is the #1 rug signal, but only if the lock is real: verify the LP tokens are in a known lock contract (Unicrypt, Team Finance, or a verified custom lock), check the unlock date, and confirm the lock contract cannot be bypassed (e.g. no owner function to withdraw early, no upgrade path). A 'locked' claim with LP tokens still in the deployer wallet, or in an unverified lock contract, is not a lock. Also check that the deployer cannot mint new supply to dump into the locked pool. Severity: critical.

title: Whale Tracking Heuristics
content: Whale tracking finds large holders and their behavior: top-10 holder concentration, wallets that moved >X% of supply, accumulation vs distribution patterns, exchange inflows/outflows, and cross-wallet clustering (funding from the same source = same entity). Whales with unlocked positions near a token's peak are distribution risk; whales accumulating through fresh addresses can hide intent. Combine on-chain flow with funding and OI for a full picture. Severity: informational.

title: Lockup Bypass and Unlock Cliff Red Flags
content: Token lockups are only as strong as their enforcement: a lock the deployer can unlock, a 'vesting' contract that can be bypassed by minting new supply, or an unlock cliff that dumps a large percentage at once all create sell pressure. Red flags: team tokens locked in a wallet the team controls (they can move them), 'locked' claims unverifiable on-chain, and unlock schedules with a single massive cliff instead of linear vesting. Monitor the vesting contract's actual mechanics, not the announcement. Severity: high.

title: Revenue vs Emissions: Real Yield vs Inflation
content: A token's sustainability is revenue minus emissions: if a protocol mints more token value than it earns in fees, holders are subsidizing the deficit and the token slowly bleeds. Compute fee value vs emission value per period; APYs paid in minted tokens are only 'real' if buy pressure from actual usage offsets the dilution. Projects hide this with 'buyback' narratives that buy less than they mint. On-chain check: compare protocol fee flows against mint events. Severity: high.

title: Low Float / High FDV Launch Dynamics
content: A 'low float, high FDV' launch sells a small circulating supply against a huge fully-diluted valuation: price looks strong because float is tiny, but the FDV overhang means future unlocks can crush price. The ratio (FDV / market cap) reveals the overhang: 10x+ means 90% of supply unlocks later. Compare circulating vs total supply and map the unlock calendar to actual dates. VC round prices also set a floor reference for early investors who can dump. Severity: medium.

title: Intents and Solver-Based Settlement
content: Intents let users express WHAT they want (swap A for B at limit price) rather than HOW (transaction path), and solvers compete to fulfill them. Intent-based settlement (as in CoW/EigenLayer-style auctions, ERC-7683 cross-chain intents) reduces MEV and improves prices, but shifts trust to solvers and introduces new failure modes: solver insolvency, filler collusion, and relay censorship. For analysis, an 'intent' architecture means the executed path differs from a normal tx — check the filler and the settlement contract. Severity: informational.

title: Smart Accounts, Session Keys and Passkeys
content: ERC-4337 smart accounts (account abstraction) enable social recovery, spending limits, batching and session keys — long-lived permissions that let a dApp act for a user within limits. Session keys are powerful and dangerous: a compromised session key can drain within its scope, and phishing targets signature prompts. Passkeys (WebAuthn) improve key hygiene but move trust to the authenticator vendor. When analyzing a smart-account wallet, review its module/guardian set and session-key permissions. Severity: medium.

title: Liquid Staking Derivatives (LSD) Mechanics
content: Liquid staking derivatives (stETH, etc.) represent staked ETH plus accruing rewards; they let staked capital stay liquid and composable. Risks: de-peg from the underlying (exchange-rate drift), withdrawal queue delays, slashing of validators, and protocol concentration. LSDs back a large share of DeFi borrowing, so an LSD de-peg can cascade into lending liquidations. Check the staking protocol's withdrawal mechanics, validator distribution, and historical peg stability. Severity: medium.

title: Bridge Taxonomy: Trust Models Compared
content: Bridges fall into trust models with very different risk: (1) lock-and-mint with a validator set (Ronin/Wormhole-style) — risk = validator compromise; (2) optimistic bridges with a challenge window (fraud proofs) — risk = watcher liveness and challenge economics; (3) light-client / zk-proof bridges (trustless) — risk = proving bugs and implementation flaws. Historical losses concentrate in the validator-compromise class. The security of a bridge equals the security of its weakest trust component; check the model before trusting a wrapped asset. Severity: high.

title: Long and Short Squeeze Mechanics
content: A short squeeze forces short sellers to buy back as price rises, accelerating the move; a long squeeze (long liquidation cascade) forces leveraged longs to sell as price falls, accelerating the crash. Squeezes are driven by liquidations, funding-rate extremes, and clustered stops. Signals: extreme funding, elevated open interest vs market cap, and liquidation clusters at known levels. In crypto, squeezes on low-float tokens are routinely manufactured by coordinated players. Severity: informational.

title: Listing Pump and Dump Patterns
content: A CEX or DEX listing is a liquidity event that attracts FOMO buyers — and an exit opportunity for insiders. The listing-pump pattern: price spikes on the listing announcement/execution, insiders sell into the new liquidity, price dumps once buying exhausts. On-chain tells: large deposits to the exchange right before the listing and heavy sell-side flow in the first hours. A 'listing' is not validation of a project; verify the listing venue's diligence and the token's on-chain behavior independent of the announcement. Severity: informational.
